Four of the six titles are the Vulgate's own word, lifted from the verse printed beside them. Tit. ii. 14 *ut mundaret sibi populum* gives `mundator`; Heb. ii. 15 *ut liberaret eos* gives `liberator`; Col. ii. 15 *palam triumphans illos* gives `triumphator`; Heb. vi. 20 *ubi præcursor … introivit Iesus* gives `præcursor`, the only place the word occurs in the New Testament. The catalogue is quarried, not composed. Exactly two depart, and both depart somewhere. Rom. viii. 34 says only *interpellat pro nobis*; `Advocatus` is at 1 John ii. 1. And Heb. xii. 2 reads *auctorem fidei et consummatorem* where the plate sets `Instaurator` — the verb of Eph. i. 10, *instaurare omnia in Christo*. At the second Advent the title is not the finisher of our faith but the restorer of all things; the English keeps "finisher" because the reference is to Hebrews and Part III renders it so.

§32 begins here, and its heading is a technical word. Ἀνακεφαλαίωσις is the noun of Eph. i. 10's *ἀνακεφαλαιώσασθαι*, to gather all things under one head in Christ — Irenæus' term, not a synonym for "summary." What it gathers is the Creed stripped to its events, Conception to Judgement, with no doctrine and no Church among them; and it closes not *credo* but *Fac me horum participem*, make me partaker of them.

Four sins against the Spirit, and each is a different verb from a different book. *Quench* is 1 Thessalonians v. 19 · *strive against* is Stephen's *ye do always resist the Holy Ghost*, Acts vii. 51 · *grieve* is Ephesians iv. 30 · *do despite* is Hebrews x. 29, *hath done despite unto the Spirit of grace*. A reader with only the English will hear a rhetorical heap where the plate has four distinct scriptural offences, gathered from four books and set in ascending order of gravity. None is a synonym for another.
